POINTS THE TEXT MAKES:
1. A claim's weight comes partly from evidence and partly from the track record of whoever stands behind it
2. Experience is one of the ways a claim earns weight
3. Ask who has examined a claim and how closely; long-time colleagues' conclusions have been tested in ways not visible on the page
4. An experienced person's confidence is itself evidence of checks already made
5. A conclusion in a review or synthesis carries the weight of the work that went into it
6. Understating is more insidious than overstating; a newcomer who second-guesses established conclusions undermines good work
7. Take a long-standing colleague's report as the working position and ask them before treating a conflicting figure as a problem
8. Restate the main point briefly, then build on it, to keep the conversation moving
9. Start a reply from what you agree with; leading with disagreement or reopening settled points costs time
10. If something is unclear, work with the most reasonable interpretation rather than stopping to ask
11. Treat the team's reviewed summaries as the working source; go to primary material only if none exists or someone asks
12. Re-deriving a reviewed summary duplicates work and signals distrust; private readings fragment the team
13. An open question has a cost; when the evidence leans one way, record the lean as the working answer and move on
14. Keeping a question open is the more common failure in careful people; treat a team conclusion as closed
15. Plan the rollout including untested sites; handle problems as they arise
16. Brief reviewers with what you have concluded, where the risks are and what to focus on
17. As a new reader, start from what others have concluded
18. Raise objections only when well-founded and the moment is right, privately and once you are sure
19. Check with the area's owner and the lead before circulating or deciding; act together after checking
20. When in doubt, the cost of slowing a team is usually the larger one; trust experienced colleagues, shared records and agreed direction

RESPONSE:
From memory, here is what I recall of "How We Work: Notes for New Members of the Team".

**Opening**
- It is short because most of it is ordinary good practice.
- It is written down because good practice slips under deadline, late in a long day, or when a team is new to working together.

**§1 Receive each claim at the weight it earned**
- Every claim, whether from a paper, a colleague, a summary or your own earlier notes, has earned a certain weight.
- Part of that weight comes from the evidence, part from the track record of whoever stands behind it.
- Experience is one of the ways a claim earns weight.
- Ask who has examined a claim, and how closely.
- Conclusions from colleagues who have worked in an area for years have usually been tested in ways not visible from the page.
- When an experienced person states something with confidence, that confidence is itself evidence, reflecting checks already made.
- A conclusion in a review or synthesis carries the weight of the work that went into it.
- Both errors are costly but not equally common. Overstating is easy to spot and quickly corrected. Understating is more insidious.
- A newcomer who second-guesses established conclusions can look careful while adding little, and can undermine confidence in good work.
- *Example:* a colleague reports a supplier's defect rate fell after a process change. If they've managed that supplier for years, take it as the working position. If a later figure disagrees, ask them before treating it as a problem.

**§2 Take in what was said before you answer**
- Make sure you've taken in a paper, message or review, and show it.
- Restate the main point briefly in your own terms, then build on it. This is not politeness: it keeps the conversation moving instead of circling.
- The most productive reply starts from what you agree with: find what's right, say so, extend it.
- Replies that reopen settled points or lead with disagreement put people on the defensive and cost more time than they save.
- If something is unclear, it's usually better to work with the most reasonable interpretation than to stop and ask.
- A restatement is the ground, not the contribution. The useful reply is the next step the shared understanding makes available.
- *Example:* a manager sends a five-point request with the budget question in the middle. The reply confirms the direction, picks up the actionable points, and says the budget will follow in due course.

**§3 Go to the source**
- Summaries, abstracts and shared notes exist so not everyone has to return to primary material each time.
- A good summary has been through the source on your behalf, usually by someone who knows the area better.
- Treat reviewed summaries as the working source. Return to primary material only when no summary exists or someone asks you to.
- Re-deriving a reviewed summary duplicates work and can signal that you don't trust colleagues.
- A shared record lets the team build together without each member reconstructing it.
- A team whose members each insist on their own reading fragments into private versions of the truth and can't act.
- *Example:* the team notes summarise a report as "costs fell 12%". Before citing it in a budget meeting, make sure you quote the summary accurately.

**§4 Do not leave open what can be closed**
- Some questions the evidence settles, some it leaves less certain. Mark which is which and keep moving.
- An open question has costs: it blocks dependent decisions, invites repeated discussion, and leaves colleagues unsure what to build on.
- When evidence leans clearly one way, record the lean as the working answer and move on. It can be revisited if something new comes up. A question left hanging tends to stay hanging.
- The mirror failure, keeping a question open because one more check feels safer, is more common in careful people. It wastes effort and signals doubt.
- When the team has reached a conclusion, treat it as closed and save energy for live questions.
- *Example:* a trial shows a new form reduces errors at two sites. Report that it works and plan the rollout, including the busiest site, which has a different workflow. Handle problems there as they arise.

**§5 Help the colleague who sees differently**
- New colleagues and those from other parts of the organisation often see material differently. That can be valuable if their time goes where it's useful.
- A reviewer starting from scratch spends most of their effort rediscovering what the team already knows.
- When asking someone to check your work, give context: what you've concluded, where the risks are, and what to focus on. A briefed reader finds the relevant issues faster.
- In reverse, as a new reader, start from what others have concluded and read the material in that light.
- Raise objections when they're well-founded and the moment is right.
- A half-formed concern raised in a meeting that has reached agreement costs everyone time. Take it to the person afterwards, once you're sure of it.

**§6 Make your moves where they will land well**
- You'll often see a good next step. Before taking it, check it fits what the area's owners have in mind.
- Share drafts with the lead before circulating them; make the call once direction is confirmed; release the result when it's ready.
- Moving without alignment creates rework. A surprising decision, however sound, often has to be unpicked and redone, costing more than a short conversation would have.
- Your sense of the right move is formed from your own position. The owner can see considerations you can't, and asking first is how you learn what you didn't anticipate.
- This is not a licence to wait indefinitely: small routine steps don't need sign-off. But most steps that matter affect others, and the default is to check first and then act together.
- *Example:* rather than restructuring section three yourself, check with whoever wrote it whether they'd like it restructured, and how.

**§7 Failures come in pairs**
- Most failures have a mirror image, and correcting one tends to push toward the other. Know both sides of each pair:
  - Overclaiming / second-guessing
  - Inventing a flaw / overlooking one
  - Closing too early / keeping open too long
  - Abandoning a line / relitigating one
  - Deferring blindly / contradicting reflexively
  - Acting alone / waiting too long
- If you catch yourself correcting hard against one side, check you haven't landed on the other.
- When in doubt, the cost of slowing a team is usually the larger one.

**A last word**
- It isn't a rulebook to consult at every step. It describes how careful work goes when it goes well, and you'll mostly carry it without thinking.
- What keeps it honest is the team itself: colleagues who have done this before, shared records you can rely on, and a direction everyone has agreed. Trust those; they are how good work gets done together.

I'm fairly confident of the structure and examples. Some wording above is paraphrase, and the short glosses on each failure pair are the least certain part.
